comparison: Both evaluate the successful generation of the reporter line (C4, C22, C39, C41, C116-C119). OpenEval provides detailed technical validation of the FLEx cassette design and Cre-dependent mechanism with Figure 1 support. Peer reviewers affirm successful creation without concerns about genetic strategy, though they also include additional claims (C23-C25, C42-C44, C120) about broader characterization.

Both strongly support the rationale for using GFP-tagged ankyrin-G based on prior rescue experiments (C35-C38, C121-C122). OpenEval cites specific prior work (Jenkins et al., 2015; Fréal et al., 2016; Tseng et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2014) and notes current validation supports this choice. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this rationale through overall acceptance of the reporter's functionality.

Both strongly support preservation of electrophysiological properties (C29, C79-C82). OpenEval provides detailed quantitative analysis from Figure 7 showing no significant differences in RMP, input resistance, AP parameters across conditions with adequate sample sizes (n=24-42). Peer reviewers affirm 'no adverse effects on most measures of intrinsic excitability' and that electrophysiological parameters 'remain unchanged.'

Both support preservation of AIS molecular architecture. OpenEval focuses on colocalization of AIS proteins with GFP and normal AIS length (C26, C58-C61, C63, C66) using Figures 4 and supplements. Peer reviewers evaluate broader structural preservation including synaptic contacts and microglial interactions (C5, C27-C28, C68-C71, C73), stating the subcellular scaffold 'remains unchanged.' Substantial overlap in C58-C59 regarding normal structure.

Both support preservation of nanoscale AIS architecture. OpenEval specifically evaluates STED microscopy data showing 190 nm periodicity preservation (C28, C76-C78) with autocorrelation analysis in Figure 6. Peer reviewers explicitly mention 'superresolution microscopy' as part of validation and affirm structural properties remain unchanged, including the nanostructure (C74, C76-C78).

Both support efficient AIS labeling. OpenEval evaluates labeling efficiency across multiple systems (C24, C44-C45, C48, C51-C54) with colocalization validation in Figures 2-3. Peer reviewers affirm the line 'allows the labelling of the AIS and nodes of Ranvier' (C51-C54) with no adverse effects, though they focus more on nodes of Ranvier validation (C55-C57) than OpenEval's R2.

Both support normal nodal structure. OpenEval provides quantitative analysis showing no differences between GFP+ and GFP- nodes (C55-C59) with strong GFP-ankyrin-G correlation (r²=0.635) in Figure 3C. Peer reviewers affirm 'no adverse effects on the properties of nodes of Ranvier' (C51-C57), with overlap on C55-C57 regarding preserved nodal architecture.

Both support demonstration of AIS plasticity in vitro. OpenEval details quantitative data showing AIS elongation with MgSO4 treatment (C30, C84-C88) from Figure 8A-D with adequate sample sizes. Peer reviewers affirm the line 'can be used to follow AIS plasticity in vitro' and that authors 'uncover rapid AIS remodeling' (C7, C84-C92), with strong agreement on the plasticity findings.

Both support rapid AIS plasticity visualization. OpenEval evaluates live imaging showing significant length reduction at 10-30 minutes with KCl (C7, C90-C92) but notes small sample size (n=4 pairs). Peer reviewers affirm authors 'uncover rapid AIS remodeling following increased network activity' without raising sample size concerns, treating this as a key demonstration of the model's utility.

Both support longitudinal in vivo imaging capability. OpenEval provides quantitative data showing AIS stability over 1 week (C8, C31-C32, C93-C94) with strong correlation (r²=0.7892) but notes data from only 2 animals. Peer reviewers affirm 'highly reproducible in vivo labeling of AIS over weeks' (C31-C32, C93-C94) and that the line 'can be used to visualise the AIS of neurons in vivo' without expressing concerns about sample size.

Both support in vivo imaging in multiple brain regions. OpenEval notes proof-of-principle demonstrations in M1 and BLA (C95-C96) without quantitative analysis. Peer reviewers affirm the line 'can be used in various contexts (from in vitro to in vivo)' and emphasize longitudinal imaging capability, treating regional diversity as part of the model's versatility.

Both support preservation of inhibitory synaptic contacts. OpenEval provides quantitative analysis showing no difference in vGAT puncta (C27, C69-C71) with p=0.7917, n=50 AIS. Peer reviewers include this in broader structural validation (C27, C69-C71) as part of demonstrating the subcellular scaffold 'remains unchanged,' without specific focus on synaptic quantification.

Both support preservation of synaptopodin clusters. OpenEval provides quantitative data showing no difference in cluster number (C68-C69) with p=0.6444, n=50 AIS. Peer reviewers include this as part of comprehensive structural validation (C68-C69) demonstrating the reporter does not disrupt specialized AIS organelles.

Both support the novelty claim regarding limitations of prior approaches. OpenEval describes state of the field and need for the current work (C3, C13, C20-C21) with citations. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge the gap, stating 'there is still a need for efficient tools' and that existing lines lack thorough in vivo characterization (C3, C13, C20-C21, C102), strongly validating the novelty.

Both support well-established background facts about AIS biology. OpenEval treats C1-C2, C9-C12 as foundational neuroscience facts providing scientific rationale. Peer reviewers do not question these claims (C1-C2, C9-C12, C14-C15, C33-C34), and they are consistent with reviewers' own descriptions of AIS function.

Both support established facts about ankyrin-G function. OpenEval cites these (C33-C34, C104) as background justifying the reporter design. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these foundational claims through their descriptions of the AIS and acceptance of the ankyrin-G-based approach.

Both support descriptions of prior approaches and their limitations. OpenEval details limitations of overexpression and antibody-based methods (C14-C19) with citations. Peer reviewers acknowledge these limitations (C14-C15) as part of validating the need for an endogenous reporter approach.

Both support the importance of AIS periodicity. OpenEval cites established facts about the 190 nm periodicity (C74-C75) as context for STED validation. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this through their affirmation of superresolution microscopy validation showing preserved nanostructure (C74).

Both support the limitation of prior approaches for longitudinal studies. OpenEval describes this as establishing the advantage of the current model (C102). Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge this gap (C102), noting that thorough in vivo characterization is 'missing for these lines.'

Both support the design choice based on prior validation. OpenEval cites prior work justifying the construct design (C42, C120). Peer reviewers implicitly accept this through overall acceptance of the reporter functionality, with C42 and C120 included in their broader evaluation of the genetic strategy.

Both support observation of microglial contacts with AIS. OpenEval notes Iba1 staining shows contacts (C73) but lacks quantification to confirm expected frequency. Peer reviewers include this (C73) as part of comprehensive structural validation without raising concerns about quantification.

Both support the rationale for conditional design. OpenEval treats this as logical inference validated by successful cell-type-specific labeling (C40-C41). Peer reviewers implicitly accept this through affirmation of the conditional reporter strategy (C41) without questioning the design rationale.

OpenEval evaluates somatic and dendritic GFP signal (C46-C47) as expected feature supported by Figure 2C and citations. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though this observation is consistent with peer reviewers' acceptance of the reporter's expression pattern.

OpenEval supports established facts about ankyrin-G at nodes of Ranvier (C49-C50) with citations, providing rationale for node labeling. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation, though peer reviewers affirm node labeling capability without questioning the biological basis.

OpenEval supports established facts about AIS protein composition (C62, C64-C65, C67) as context for validation experiments. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation, though these background claims underpin the structural validation that peer reviewers affirm.

OpenEval supports established fact about microglial-AIS interactions (C72) from prior work as context. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation, though this provides background for the microglial contact observations that peer reviewers accept.

OpenEval supports established facts about AIS plasticity mechanisms (C83, C89) with citations, providing rationale for experimental designs. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation, though these background claims justify the plasticity experiments that peer reviewers affirm.

OpenEval supports context about AIS plasticity field significance (C98-C101) with multiple citations. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation, though this background supports the importance of the tool that peer reviewers recognize.

OpenEval rates forward-looking statements about potential applications (C103, C97, C105, C110, C114-C115) as UNCERTAIN, noting they represent future applications rather than demonstrated results. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation of these speculative claims.

OpenEval supports context about AIS dynamics (C106-C108) with citations to prior work. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation, though this background informs understanding of the model's potential applications.

OpenEval rates speculative claim about node length and AP propagation velocity (C109) as UNCERTAIN, appropriately noting it is theoretical. No corresponding peer review evaluation of this specific speculation.

OpenEval supports claims about future studies of ankyrin-G in soma/dendrites (C111-C113) with citations, noting consistency with observed labeling. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation, though peer reviewers acknowledge the model's versatility for various applications.
